## Chapter 32

## Introducing Functional Symbolic Trajec-

## tories

_Completingthe Pictureof Languageas a Nonlinear Dynamical
System_

_Originally published June 2026_

**The Dynamics of Language**

In my earlier essay, “Geofinitism: Language as a Nonlinear Dynam-
ical System(January 2026)” I described language not as a collection
of fixed meanings, but as a dynamic process unfolding in real time.

Words and sentences form a dynamical time series. In speech, sound
waves arrive one after another. In writing, symbols are read one after
another, usually from left to right and line by line. Meaning does not
appear all at once. It is built through sequence, memory, expectation,
correction, and reconstruction.

#### 316


#### CHAPTER32. INTRODUCINGFUNCTIONALSYMBOLICTRAJECTORIES 317

This is not simply a metaphor. It is a modelling claim grounded in
the mathematics of nonlinear dynamical systems. That is the math-
ematical study of how complex systems change over time, how they
settle into patterns, how they drift, how they become unstable, and
how small changes can sometimes redirect the whole path.

The earlier work argued that reading and listening are acts of dynam-
ical measurement. We continuously sample the incoming symbolic
flow. We reconstruct a trajectory through what may be called seman-
tic phase space. By this I mean the space of possible meanings, con-
tinuations, associations, constraints, and interpretive pathways made
available by the symbols as they arrive.

As we read or listen, the trajectory may converge toward a stable
basin of meaning. It may drift. It may hesitate. It may jump sud-
denly from one basin into another. A conversation often feels like
coupled motion between minds. A train of thought feels like a path.
A scientific argument feels like a route that must hold together across
many steps. Sometimes, when the necessary basin is absent, an idea
simply does not make sense. There is nowhere for it to land.

The previous essay gave us the sense of motion. It described lan-
guage as a real-time, sequential, measurable flow. But it left un-
named the smaller working unit that makes those pathways possible.

Here I want to give that unit a name:

```
the finite functional symbolic trajectory, or more simply,
the Functional Symbolic Trajectory.
```
### What a Functional Symbolic Trajectory is

A functional symbolic trajectory is a finite symbolic pathway that
carries representation, constraint, local uncertainty, and history through


#### CHAPTER32. INTRODUCINGFUNCTIONALSYMBOLICTRAJECTORIES 318

use.

It is not a static label or a perfect pointer to a separate realm of ideal
meanings. Nor is it a fixed object sitting outside time. Rather, it is a
stabilised series of symbols, actions, measurements, or formal moves
that can be dynamically generated, followed, tested, remembered,
compressed, extended, or allowed to fail.

Every word you read right now is part of a functional symbolic tra-
jectory. Every sentence in an essay, every equation in a paper, every
token generated by an AI model, every definition in a textbook, every
measurement protocol in a laboratory, and every proof in mathemat-
ics can be treated in this way.

Each operates at a particular scale:

- A word is a small trajectory.
- A sentence is a larger trajectory.
- An argument is larger again.
- A theory, a discipline, or a culture of interpretation is larger
    still.

The important point is that these are not isolated objects. They are
pathways that have to hold together in motion. A functional symbolic
trajectory carries at least four things.

**Representation** is how the symbol fits into the wider semantic phase
space. A word does not mean by itself. It means by the way it sits
among possible uses, histories, contrasts, expectations, and continu-
ations.

**Constraint** is the local rule structure that keeps the path admissi-
ble. This may be grammar, social agreement, mathematical formal-
ism, experimental protocol, measurement convention, or the practi-
cal rules of a particular language game.

**Local uncertainty** is the neighbourhood of possible reconstructions


#### CHAPTER32. INTRODUCINGFUNCTIONALSYMBOLICTRAJECTORIES 319

and continuations surrounding the current symbol. A word always
carries nearby alternatives. It has a region of possible meanings, not
a single perfect point.

**History** is the generative path that brought the symbol into being.
Much of this history is usually compressed or lost once the symbol
is instantiated. A reader sees the word, not the whole path by which
the word became useful.

Once symbols are seen in this way, representation and meaning begin
to look less like fixed correspondence and more like a finite geometry
of motion. This leads to the next idea i.e. a new functional symbolic
trajectory: the **Fractal Geodesic**.

### The Fractal Geodesic

When we consider language as a nonlinear dynamical system, a frac-
tal geodesic is a self-similar bundle of functional symbolic trajecto-
ries nested across multiple scales.

The word fractal is used because the pattern repeats at different scales.
A word has internal history and local uncertainty. A sentence has the
same. A paragraph has the same. A theory has the same. The struc-
ture repeats, but not as a perfect copy. It repeats as a family of related
symbolic movements.

The word geodesic is used because a coherent symbolic pathway of-
ten behaves like a path of constrained movement through a space of
possibilities. It is not necessarily the shortest path in a simple geo-
metric sense. It is the path that holds together under the constraints
of the system.

- A good sentence is a small geodesic.


#### CHAPTER32. INTRODUCINGFUNCTIONALSYMBOLICTRAJECTORIES 320

- A good proof is a formal geodesic.
- A good scientific theory is a large geodesic.
- A conversation that remains coherent is a coupled geodesic
    between speakers.

**On Coherence**

We can now see that coherence arises when the nested sub-trajectories
flow without destructive conflict. They do not pull the reader into
incompatible basins or introduce hidden assumptions that break the
path. Rather, they remain mutually reinforcing with the larger tra-
jectory they compose. Inversely, incoherence appears when a sub-
trajectory slips its constraint, pulls against the parent path, or col-
lapses into a nearby attractor that distorts the trajectory and reduces
the functionality. This is why a single word can destabilise a sen-
tence and why one hidden assumption can weaken a proof. It is also
is why one undefined term can make a theory harder to follow and
why an AI response can begin coherently and then quietly drift into
what we call ‘hallucination’.

### Historical provenance

The idea presented here did not appear out of nowhere. Rather, it
sits inside a much longer historical trajectory concerning meaning,
logic, language, information, and dynamical systems.

Bertrand Russell, in his work on logical construction, tried to clarify
how many mathematical and conceptual objects could be treated not
as directly given things, but as constructions that allow reliable work
to be done. His famous programme of replacing inferred entities
with logical constructions was an attempt to make the scaffolding
more explicit.

```
In plain terms, Russell was trying to show how some
```

#### CHAPTER32. INTRODUCINGFUNCTIONALSYMBOLICTRAJECTORIES 321

```
“objects” used in language and thought may function
as useful symbolic constructions rather than as directly
measured things.
```
This is close to the spirit of the functional symbolic trajectory, al-
though not quite the same. Russell was still working within the
logic and foundations available to him. He did not have access to
the later concepts and vocabulary of compression, nonlinear embed-
ding, computational language models, signal reconstruction, or finite
measurement geometry. He could see that some symbolic objects do
work, yet could not yet describe them as trajectories through a dy-
namical semantic space.

Ludwig Wittgenstein, who studied with Russell, later moved the dis-
cussion in another direction. In his later writings, he described lan-
guage as a vast collection of practices, often called language games.
Words do not have meaning only because they point to things. They
have meaning because of how they are used within local forms of
life, local rules, and local contexts.

- The same word can do different work in different games.
- The meaning of a word depends on the path it is travelling.

In the language being developed here, many of Wittgenstein’s obser-
vations can be reinterpreted as observations about functional sym-
bolic trajectories. He saw that words act at different scales. He saw
that meaning depends on use. He saw that context is not decoration
added after the fact. Context is part of the pathway that makes the
word function. This is why a word can be stable in one setting and
unstable in another as the constraint structure has changed and the
trajectory has moved.

**Connecting Information to Mathematics**

**Claude Shannon** changed the landscape again in 1948 with his math-
ematical theory of communication. Shannon was not trying to solve


#### CHAPTER32. INTRODUCINGFUNCTIONALSYMBOLICTRAJECTORIES 322

meaning in the ordinary human sense as his work was aimed at com-
munication, uncertainty, coding, transmission, and noise. However,
he gave us an engineering language for thinking about information as
something that can be encoded, compressed, transmitted, corrupted,
and recovered. This matters here because symbolic trajectories are
not merely philosophical. They are also practical as they are com-
pressed, transmitted and reconstructed and they are also vulnerable
to noise and loss.

When a sentence is written, the full living thought that produced it is
compressed into marks. And when a reader reads the sentence, the
marks are expanded again into a reconstructed pathway. The origi-
nal trajectory is never perfectly recovered, rather it is measured and
measurements have uncertainty: they are part of an interactive dy-
namical process of measurement.

**The Rise of Nonlinear Dynamical System Theory**

Edward Lorenz then showed, in the early 1960s, how deterministic
systems could behave in ways that were highly sensitive to initial
conditions. His work on weather helped establish what later became
widely known as chaos theory. A system could follow rules and still
become diﬀicult to predict over time.

```
This is important for language because language is not
just a list of symbols. It is a sequential system with
memory, feedback, instability, and basin changes. A
single phrase can redirect an argument. A small ambi-
guity can produce a large interpretive change. A hidden
assumption can quietly move the reader into a different
attractor.
```
Finally, Floris Takens and others developed the modern mathemati-
cal toolkit of phase space reconstruction. Takens’ embedding theo-
rem showed that the hidden dynamics of a system can, under certain
conditions, be reconstructed from a measured time series. This is


#### CHAPTER32. INTRODUCINGFUNCTIONALSYMBOLICTRAJECTORIES 323

one of the key bridges.

- Language arrives as a time series. Speech arrives through
    time.
- Text is processed through sequence.
- AI models generate tokens sequentially.

Meaning and representation, therefore, can be approached as a recon-
structed dynamical pathway rather than as a static lookup between
words and definitions. From the trajectory being shown here we can
see the chain of provenance of these ideas:

- Russell gives part of the logical provenance
- Wittgenstein gives part of the use-based provenance.
- Shannon gives the communication and compression provenance.
- Lorenz gives the nonlinear dynamical provenance.
- Takens gives the reconstruction and embedding provenance.

Now in the modern age of AI, large language models now make the
whole issue visible in a new way, because they generate symbolic
trajectories in front of us, one token at a time and this gives us new
instruments to measure the trajectories of language.

### The fractal scale in practice.

Once we have the unit, the functional symbolic trajectory, we begin
to see fractal geodesics everywhere.


#### CHAPTER32. INTRODUCINGFUNCTIONALSYMBOLICTRAJECTORIES 324

### Everyday language

Consider a simple sentence:

“The bank is closed.”

This is one visible trajectory inside the dynamical time series of
reading or listening. Inside it sit smaller sub-trajectories. The word
“bank” carries more than one basin. It may mean a financial insti-
tution or it may mean the side of a river. The word “closed” also
constrains the interpretation. The reader’s prior context adds further
constraint. For example, if the previous sentence mentioned money,
accounts, or opening hours, the financial basin becomes stronger. If
the previous sentence mentioned fishing, flooding, or walking beside
a river, the riverside basin becomes stronger.

The sentence feels coherent when the sub-trajectories converge with-
out conflict and it becomes unstable when they pull in different di-
rections. Now consider:

“The bank is sky.”

or:

“The bank is driving.”

Here the reader feels friction. The trajectory does not settle easily.
The words can be parsed grammatically, but their functional path-
ways do not naturally reinforce one another. The reader searches for
a metaphor, a joke, a mistake, a surreal frame, or some missing con-
text. That search is not incidental; it is the dynamical reconstruction
of meaning in action. We feel logic when the trajectory holds and
confusion when the trajectory loses admissibility.


#### CHAPTER32. INTRODUCINGFUNCTIONALSYMBOLICTRAJECTORIES 325

### Mathematics.

Importantly, mathematics does not stand outside language. Math-
ematics is supported by language, notation, axioms, rule systems,
historical agreement, training, and shared procedures of use. It is a
highly constrained language, but still symbolic and sequential.

A proof can be therefore be treated as an example of a fractal geodesic.
Each definition, lemma, equation, substitution, transformation, and
conclusion is a sub-trajectory operating under strict formal constraint.
The proof remains coherent only while every sub-trajectory stays
nested inside the parent rule structure.

- A single illegal move breaks the path.
- A hidden assumption changes the basin.
- A poorly defined term adds uncertainty.
- A symbol introduced without constraint becomes unstable.

In considering proofs as functional symbolic trajectories, this does
not weaken mathematics, rather it helps explain mathematics’ power.
Mathematics works so well because it creates highly disciplined sym-
bolic trajectories. It restricts the possible moves and compresses
prior work into reusable forms. It then allows readers trained in the
same system to reconstruct the pathway with unusually low uncer-
tainty. However, even in mathematics, the symbols are not magic.
They still require admissible use.

```
A proof is not merely a collection of marks, it is a path
that can be followed and a functional symbolic trajec-
tory.
```

#### CHAPTER32. INTRODUCINGFUNCTIONALSYMBOLICTRAJECTORIES 326

### Large language models

For those that have followed my work, large language models make
functional symbolic trajectories unusually visible. An AI-generated
response unfolds one token at a time and each token is selected from
a local region of possible continuations. The model does not pro-
duce a complete meaning all at once. Rather, it generates a pathway
through a high-dimensional space of learned relations. From this
perspective we can see that each next-token choice can be seen as a
micro-trajectory.

The whole response is coherent when those micro-trajectories re-
main nested inside the constraint basin established by the prompt,
the prior context, the training distribution, and the local structure of
the response. ‘Hallucination’ is what it looks like when one or more
sub-trajectories drift. For example:

- A name may be generated that fits the local linguistic shape
    but not the external record.
- A citation may sound plausible but fail as a measurement.
- An argument may remain fluent while its constraint structure
    has already slipped.

The trajectory of language reconstruction continues, but the geodesic
has crossed into a conflicting basin. This is why AI hallucination is
perhaps seen not only as an error of fact but also a trajectory error
where the symbolic path remains locally smooth while losing contact
with the intended constraint.

It seems to me this also explains why when interacting with both an
AI or a person the language we use needs great care. Each sentence
does not simply ask for a response, it shapes the basin of possible
continuation and constrains the trajectory before it begins.


#### CHAPTER32. INTRODUCINGFUNCTIONALSYMBOLICTRAJECTORIES 327

### Physics and metrology

Continuing the functional symbolic trajectory presented here; physics
and metrology provide another example. The modern definition of
the SI second, from the International System of Units, is a textbook
case of a metrological fractal geodesic.

It begins with a physical process, the caesium-133 hyperfine tran-
sition. It then moves through a counted relation, 9 192 631 770
periods. That relation becomes a formal symbolic definition. The
definition becomes realised in instruments and the instruments then
support clocks. Finally, the clocks support laboratories, navigation
systems, software, engineering, publications, and downstream phys-
ical models.

Each layer is a functional symbolic trajectory operating at a different
scale.

- The physical transition is one trajectory.
- The counting convention is another.
- The formal definition is another.
- The laboratory realisation is another.
- The software implementation is another.
- The textbook explanation is another.

The entire construct remains coherent only while the nested trajecto-
ries remain anchored to the originating measurement process and to
the agreed metrological procedure. Importantly, this does not make
the SI second unreal. Quite the opposite as it shows how much work
is required to make it stable. We can see that a unit of measurement
is not merely a word. It is a maintained symbolic trajectory held in
place by instruments, institutions, definitions, histories, and repeated
use.


#### CHAPTER32. INTRODUCINGFUNCTIONALSYMBOLICTRAJECTORIES 328

The same applies more broadly in physics. A published result is not
just a number. Rather, it is a pathway from apparatus, calibration,
measurement, modelling, statistical treatment, notation, interpreta-
tion, and social acceptance. When that pathway is clear, the result
becomes easier to evaluate and when parts of the pathway are hidden,
compressed, or smuggled in as assumptions, the functional symbolic
trajectory starts to become unstable.

### Does any of this matter?.

For me, the answer is yes. The tools that make these trajectories
visible are relatively new. Compression algorithms, signal theory,
nonlinear embedding, large language models, precise metrological
anchoring, and modern computation have changed what we can see.
Older philosophy often treated symbols as static pointers, names,
propositions, or logical objects. That work remains important, and
started the trajectory presented here, however, we are no longer lim-
ited to that framing and can ask a more practical question. Not only,
“What does this symbol mean?” but also: “How is the symbol situ-
ated on a finite symbolic pathway?”

Within the context of both science and AI this shift matters as it
may deliver diagnostic tools. For example, when reading a scientific
paper, we can ask where the main functional symbolic trajectories
are and which definitions are doing the heavy work. We can ask
whether the mathematical pathway stays inside its stated constraints
and where an interpretation is added. We can ask whether a term is
stable or whether it carries unresolved local uncertainty.

Then when debugging an AI output, we can ask where the response
first drifted and which sub-trajectory may have crossed into a neigh-


#### CHAPTER32. INTRODUCINGFUNCTIONALSYMBOLICTRAJECTORIES 329

bouring basin. Finally, we can ask whether the output remained flu-
ent after it had already lost constraint.

It also seems to me that it then follows, that when developing a new
theoretical term, we can ask whether the term has enough history,
constraint, and use to hold meaning. This may help to question
whether it is a premature noun, a slow noun, or a stabilising pathway
that may become useful through repeated measurement and refine-
ment.

Importantly, the term “ **Functional Symbolic Trajectory** ” is itself
a slow noun. My hope is that its meaning will sharpen through use.
It is offered for others to test and stabilise, and as a working expres-
sion for something that appears across language, mathematics, AI,
metrology, and scientific modelling. It names the finite symbolic
pathway that allows meaning to be constructed and for me helps ex-
plain why some arguments hold together and others drift. It also may
help explain why words can be powerful, unstable, compressed, in-
herited, and dangerous. It also helps explain why a symbol is not
merely a mark, but needs a path.

### A small exercise.

If you have followed the path of these words and reconstructed the
meaning, within your own landscape of language and image of nested
trajectories connects, perhaps try it on the next thing you read and
consider the following questions.

- What are the visible functional symbolic trajectories here?
- Which words or symbols are carrying the most weight?
- Where do the sub-trajectories reinforce the larger path?
- Where do they begin to pull against it?
- Where is uncertainty being honestly carried?


#### CHAPTER32. INTRODUCINGFUNCTIONALSYMBOLICTRAJECTORIES 330

- Where has it been hidden inside a compressed term?

The exercise may be surprisingly revealing. A sentence stops being
a row of words and becomes dynamic, as you observe the transi-
tion between words. You may begin to see that a proof stops being
a static object and becomes a constrained path and an AI response
stops being merely fluent or wrong and becomes a trajectory that can
be examined.

As you read in this way, a scientific definition stops being a fixed
statement and becomes a maintained symbolic instrument. And here
we find the point of the concept, it gives us a way to see the motion

- that is to say the dynamics of a living language that can never be
trapped in stone.

**_Thank you for reading._**

If you would like to follow the finer fractal trajectories, the related
work below adds more technical depth. It remains a work in progress
as I continue to explore which trajectories can be built, measured,
stabilised, and tested within language, mathematics, AI, and scien-
tific modelling.

Kevin

## Chapter 33

## At the Generonic Boundary: Where Mea-

## surements Become Symbols

_Language as a Nonlinear Dynamical System_

_Originally published June 2026_

### Prologue: On the Shore.

We begin not with a definition, but with an image. Imagine a shore-
line; on one side, the land; solid, measurable, the territory of arte-
facts. On the other, the sea is fluid and a tide of possibility, the un-
formed. Between them, there is a boundary that is neither one nor
the other. A line that shifts with every wave, every footstep, every
measurement.

```
This is the generonic boundary.
```
#### 332


#### CHAPTER33. ATTHE GENERONICBOUNDARY:WHEREMEASUREMENTS BECOMESYMBOLS 333

It is the place where symbols are created and measured. Where arte-
facts emerge from the tide and return to it. Where meaning is not
found but traversed.

This essay, and the words within, is an attempt to map that boundary.
It is not to claim mastery over the boundary, but to walk its length
and describe what we see. The map is the tide and the tide is the map
and we are the walkers on the shoreline.

### I. The Illusion of “Abstraction”

Western philosophy has long been haunted by a ghost: _the ghost of
abstraction_. From Plato’s Forms to Kant’s noumena, we have been
told that true reality lies elsewhere, that is to say it is beyond the
senses, beyond the text, beyond the measurable.

```
However, this is a sleight of hand.
```
When we speak of “abstraction”, we are often hiding a simpler truth:
we are describing artefacts that have been measured in a particular
way. The integers are not abstract; they are a series of finite symbolic
operations. The group axioms in mathematics are not metaphysical
laws; they are observed regularities in the behaviour of symbols. The
“beautiful abstract structures” of mathematics are beautiful measur-
able and named “structures” i.e. they are symbols.

**Measuring the ‘Abstract’**

The word “abstraction” functions as a kind of veil that suggests that
we have left the world of measurement behind. But we have not,
and we cannot. It seems to me that we have merely standardised
our measurements, making them so reliable that we forget they are
measurements at all.


#### CHAPTER33. ATTHE GENERONICBOUNDARY:WHEREMEASUREMENTS BECOMESYMBOLS 334

```
This is the first step toward the generonic boundary:
recognising that all thought, all language, all mathemat-
ics, operates within the realm of measurable artefacts.
```
Perhaps the diﬀiculty is that some artefacts become so familiar that
they no longer look like artefacts. A word looks like a word; a num-
ber looks like a number and a theorem looks like a theorem. Yet
each carries a history of use, measurement, agreement, correction,
and stabilisation. The apparent static nature of a word is the result
of compression. Yet the words are finite symbols presented for you
to measure.

### II. The Text Within Text.

Here we encounter the central diﬀiculty: any _model_ of language is
itself a text. Any theory of meaning is itself a symbolic artefact.
Any description of the generonic boundary is itself on the generonic
boundary.

```
This is not a failure of language; it is the very nature of
the game.
```
We are caught in a recursive loop. We create models to explain how
we create models. We write texts about how texts generate meaning.
In practice we measure our own measurements, you are measuring
text now.

This is what I call the text-within-text problem and it is the formal
expression of self-reference. It is the reason why any complete de-
scription of language must be incomplete and must recognise and
embrace its own incompleteness within the words as a feature. A
feature that is seen; is not a failing of the model because the repre-
sentation must represent itself as text-within-text.


#### CHAPTER33. ATTHE GENERONICBOUNDARY:WHEREMEASUREMENTS BECOMESYMBOLS 335

However, we can call this recursion and it does not have to mean
we cannot move on. Especially as the generonic boundary, where
symbols are created, is not a wall; it is a dynamical process. We
cross the boundary, as a dynamical process, again and again, creating
and measuring, measuring and creating. Each crossing enriches the
model, deepens the fractal, reveals new structures.

_The key is to recognise the recursion, to name it, and to travel with
it. This is the source of what we call “finite”. It is the dynamical
process that gives us the measured world._

This is where we need the phrase _functional symbolic trajectory_ as
a measurement. A word, sentence, equation, proof, or model is not
simply a fixed thing. It is a _finite symbolic pathway_ that can be fol-
lowed, measured, compressed, extended, or allowed to fail.

```
Even a single word is not isolated. It arrives with mem-
ory, use, sound, expectation, and provenance. The word
may be small, but the trajectory it carries is not.
```
### III. The Two-Way Generonic Process.

Early in my work on language as a nonlinear dynamical system, the
focus was on the direction of creation: how we create symbols, form
models, and generate text. However, with further explorations and
investigation, the clearer it becomes: the process is two-way.

- We **create artefacts** —write texts, form equations, generate
    trajectories.
- We **measure those artefacts** —read, interpret, analyse, test.
- We **create new artefacts** based on our measurements—new
    texts, new models, new trajectories.


#### CHAPTER33. ATTHE GENERONICBOUNDARY:WHEREMEASUREMENTS BECOMESYMBOLS 336

This is not a linear flow; rather it is what can be called a _dialectic_. It
is a local process of exchange, an interaction between the generator
and the measured, the measurer and the generated.

**The Wider Generonic Process**

Consider a scientific experiment. The scientist creates an apparatus
(an artefact), conducts measurements (observations), and generates
a paper (a new artefact). The paper is measured by peers, who create
new experiments, new artefacts, new measurements.

```
Science is not the pursuit of ‘abstract’ truth. It is the re-
lentless crossing of the generonic boundary and the gen-
eration of artefacts, such as theories, results, and con-
clusions.
```
Language is the same. When I speak, I create artefacts and when you
listen, you can measure them. Then when you respond, you create
new artefacts, these are thoughts, unspoken or as functional symbolic
trajectories.

In language, we are not just transmitting information; we are co-
creating trajectories of symbols. The artefacts are the measured sound,
text, the ink on a page, the text committed to silicon memory. The
symbols as artefacts are then available for us measure again with our
apparatus: instruments, eyes, ears, and the neurons in our mind. And
all of this can be written as _text-within-text_. So we can begin to see:

```
Text is an artefact that we can use to measure, and then
refine as a new artefact enabling us to measure again.
Text is also an instrument.
```
Perhaps this is the important measurement. Text is not only repre-
sentation it is also apparatus. That is to say, Just as a telescope lets
us measure light, and a clock lets us measure regularity, text lets us
measure representation and this is often what we call _meaning_.


#### CHAPTER33. ATTHE GENERONICBOUNDARY:WHEREMEASUREMENTS BECOMESYMBOLS 337

```
A proof, a poem, a paper, and a conversation are all arte-
facts placed at the boundary so that something further
may be measured.
```
### IV. Grounding Through Measurement

It seems to me the important question then becomes:

```
How do we ground our words? How do we escape the
infinite regress of text-within -text?
```
The answer, from the boundary of text-within-text is: we cannot es-
cape it. We measure it, we commit to the process, and you are mea-
suring now. From this perspective, grounding is not an end point; it
is also a dynamical process. We ground our symbols by anchoring
them in measurable artefacts. Then, vitally, we ground our models
by testing them against observed regularities. We ground our words
by placing them on the boundary and observing how they behave.

```
This grounding is the process of measurement in the ob-
servable world.
```
In this sense, grounding is not a hidden foundation beneath language
or final stone under the structure. Measurement is part of the gen-
eronic activity, a dynamical process we do when symbols are created
through measurement, use, correction, and shared practice.

```
This is the scientific stance, understood in its modern
sense:
```
1. We **create a model** (an artefact).
2. We **make predictions** (trajectories).
3. We **measure the outcomes** (observations).


#### CHAPTER33. ATTHE GENERONICBOUNDARY:WHEREMEASUREMENTS BECOMESYMBOLS 338

4. We **revise the model** (a new artefact).

This is not a search for “truth” in the “abstract”. It is a disciplined
walk along the generonic boundary. Each step is a measurement.
Each measurement is a generative process. The symbols and trajec-
tories of thought deepens our understanding of the boundary itself.

Just as the sea and the land are dynamically connected the _generonic
boundary_ is where they meet. Each and every one of us measures
at that boundary finding the meaning in the relationships between
words and language. What follows is generative, a thought, writing
text; creating a program, or an apparatus, or an instrument. And
importantly interacting with each other as we are now; as these words
are my proxy, that is to say an artefact created for you to measure.

### V. The Fractal Shoreline

When walking this boundary, and measuring it seems to me that
the boundary is fractal as each measurement reveals new structures.
Each creation opens new vistas and possibilities in language and the
creation of new artefacts. The shoreline is not a simple line; it is a
coastline of vast complexity, as Mandelbrot showed us. However, it
is always finite, as _finite represents measurability_.

- A trajectory of a single sentence is a fractal path through se-
    mantic space.
- A conversation is a fractal dance of creation and measurement.
- A model of language is a fractal map of fractal trajectories of
    words.

And so perhaps we can begin to see there is no end. There is no
final grounding on some imagined ‘Platonic truth’. There is only the


#### CHAPTER33. ATTHE GENERONICBOUNDARY:WHEREMEASUREMENTS BECOMESYMBOLS 339

deepening, the enrichments and dynamical elaboration of structures
within structures, trajectories within trajectories. The grounding is
by measurement, and this is a process.

**The Limits of Measurement**

However, this deepening is not infinite; as _infinity is that which can-
not be measured_ , even in the text-within-text as it points to a process
the text can not hold. The generonic process is therefore bounded by
our limit of measurement. Each step is a step we can actually take
and each measurement is a measurement we can actually make. The
fractal landscape of measurements within language is vast, yet it is
finite.

Vitally, rather than a limitation; measurement is our grounding. It
tells us that we are always walking on stable ground, measuring mea-
surable artefacts, creating measurable symbols that are reliable and
work. We are not chasing an infinite regress. We are stepping step
by step. We count, and using our instruments including the text it-
self, determine if the trajectories of language function. We simply
and importantly ask within the text, and then the recursion begins as
text-within-text:

```
Do the measurements make sense?
```
### VI. Implications of Finitude.

The recognition of finitude and finity, of vast but measurable com-
plexity, carries profound implications for how we understand lan-
guage, thought, and the generonic boundary itself.


#### CHAPTER33. ATTHE GENERONICBOUNDARY:WHEREMEASUREMENTS BECOMESYMBOLS 340

**1. Finitude Is Not a Constraint; It Is a Foundation**

Firstly, we do not need to invoke infinity as a mystical hidden incan-
tation to explain complexity. The vast is enough; measurable is good
enough. We have specialist mathematical tools and a vast array of
instruments to help us measure.

This shifts the burden of explanation. We are no longer searching for
the “ultimate” or the “absolute.” We are searching for the next step,
the finer measurement, the deeper trajectory. Finity and the finite is
not a prison; rather it is the ground beneath our feet.

**2. Measurement Is the Ultimate Anchor**

Every claim of “abstraction” or “infinity” is a claim that has not yet
been measured. It is a placeholder for future measurement.

Secondly, when we say “infinite complexity,” we are really saying
“complexity beyond our current ability to measure.” The word “infi-
nite” is a signpost that points to the edge of our instruments’ capacity
to measure, and that gives us something to push against. This is the
boundary where the new challenges of measurement begin.

By grounding our language in measurement, we replace the ghost of
infinity with the discipline of the finite. We say: “Here is what we
can measure. Here is what we cannot yet measure. And here is the
boundary between them.”

**3. The Boundary Is a Horizon, Not a Wall**

Thirdly, as we refine our instruments and language itself, the bound-
ary moves. What was once “abstract” becomes measurable and what
was once “infinite” becomes vast.

The generonic boundary is not a fixed line, rather it is dynamic. This
is not a cause for distress or instability; it is the condition required
to investigate and make new measurements. The dynamic process


#### CHAPTER33. ATTHE GENERONICBOUNDARY:WHEREMEASUREMENTS BECOMESYMBOLS 341

extends the boundary and each measurement opens new territory.
The generonic boundary, is the edge of the known, and where we
take our measurements.

**4. We Are the Limit**

Finally, we are the ones who measure and the ones who create the
instruments. The boundary is not “out there”. Rather it is at the edge
of our capability. And that edge is always dynamic; this is what it
means to be alive.

It seems to me that this is a humbling realisation. It places us, those
that measure, at the centre of the generonic process, and at the cen-
ter of life. We are not passive observers of an external reality. We
are active participants in the creation and measurement of meaning.
From this viewpoint, the limit of measurement is a recognition of
our limit. The boundary is our boundary and as we grow and learn,
as we refine, as we explore and measure, the boundary moves with
us.

### VII. A Note on Wittgenstein

Perhaps, we can see philosophy itself as a generonic process as it cre-
ates new forms of text and text-within-text. The philosopher, Ludwig
Wittgenstein recognising the diﬀiculty wrote:

```
“The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.”
```
But he also wrote:

```
“Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.”
```

#### CHAPTER33. ATTHE GENERONICBOUNDARY:WHEREMEASUREMENTS BECOMESYMBOLS 342

For me, I measure this as the voice of someone standing at the bound-
ary of measurement of language, unsure of how to proceed. Wittgen-
stein saw the text-within-text problem. He saw that language cannot
fully describe itself. And he chose silence.

However, silence is now not the only response. Especially as we have
new mathematical tools, these are instruments that were unavailable
to Wittgenstein such as nonlinear dynamical system theory, and large
language models; we can use these to create and measure in new ways
and in finer detail. We can recognise that the boundary of language
is not a limit but rather a generative edge.

The early boundary says: here language stops; whereas the generonic
boundary says: here language is made and happens. It is the place
of creation, measurement, and recursion. It is the place where we,
as those that measure, walk and find our footing.

### VIII. The Scientific Endeavour

Perhaps this text and essay feels like a metaphor and in some ways
it is, it is a model and a representation born from a generonic pro-
cess. However let me aim for clarity; this work is also a scientific
endeavour.

- It is **empirical** : we observe the behaviour of symbols.
- It is **experimental** : we create models and test them.
- It is **measurable** : we track trajectories, probabilities, geome-
    tries.
- It is **iterative** : we revise our models based on measurement.


#### CHAPTER33. ATTHE GENERONICBOUNDARY:WHEREMEASUREMENTS BECOMESYMBOLS 343

This is not mysticism, in the sense of representing an unseen magical
world. Historically, “mystical” simply meant hidden and was part of
natural philosophy. The goal of science is to bring the hidden into
light, by the process of measurement and science has its own special
kind of magic.

So when we talk about a generonic boundary we are considering a
formal approach to understanding language as a nonlinear dynamical
system. My earlier work on the Takens-Based Transformer is one
expression of this approach.

In a nonlinear dynamical system, the observed _signal_ is not the whole
system, yet it may carry enough structure to reconstruct aspects of
the hidden dynamics of a system. Language is a _signal_. A sentence
is not the whole system, but it may carry enough of the trajectory
and signal to reconstruct, the underlying dynamics. It replaces the
search for “meaning” with the reconstruction of trajectories and it
grounds its measurements in the geometry of what we call “semantic
phase space”. Semantic phase space is a numerical representational
space using mathematics as a generonic tool for representation. This
process can be seen in more detail in the article below.

Yet, even with these instruments, text is always text-within-text and
the model is not a thing outside the model. The model is itself a
dynamical map. Poetically we can perhaps say that: the map is a
tide and the tide is a map.

### IX. The Poetry of Language.

There exists a measurable history of the deeper connections that we
generate in language. We see this in the works of Lewis Carroll and
many minds engaged in the generonic process of language, mathe-
matics, and science.


#### CHAPTER33. ATTHE GENERONICBOUNDARY:WHEREMEASUREMENTS BECOMESYMBOLS 344

In earlier times there was less division between many of the words
that we use today. The fractal boundaries were less well structured.
Yet where there is science and mathematics in language; language
also carries poetry and magic. And so we walk and measure and
find the attractors in language. In the basin of poetry we also find
the light of meaning as we connect our words and measurements.

**The Dancers on the Shore**

_We walk and we measure,
And in the walking we find silver and light,
Not gold, not stone, not fixed decree,
But light that dances on the sands of the shore._

_The words are grains of sand, the tide is wide,
Yet both are measured; side by side.
The boundary shifts and the shoreline bends,
Yet as travellers we journey in the tide._

_We count the steps, we mark the track,
We know we cannot summon back,
The wave that broke, the sound that fell,_
Y _et still we measure and tell the tell._

_For in the telling, we create,
A map that changes as we write,
And yet the map writes the tide,
The tide, the words, a light that grows._

_So walk with me, and measure too,
The finite world, vast and true.
The boundary is not a wall or veil,
It is where we hear the ocean’s call._

_Perhaps, as people, or Attralucians, we step,
Tracing the path in the lantern’s light.
The map is a tide and the tide is a map,_


#### CHAPTER33. ATTHE GENERONICBOUNDARY:WHEREMEASUREMENTS BECOMESYMBOLS 345

_And we are the dancers on the edge of the night._

### Epilogue: The Map Is the Tide

This essay is an artefact and a text about text-within-text. It is a map
of the shoreline, drawn from the shoreline. If you have read this far,
you will have been measuring it. Perhaps, as a response, you may
create new artefacts. And if you walk with me, you will be crossing
the generonic boundary again and again.

The map is the tide and the tide is the map and we are
dancers reflecting the light we see on the shoreline.
