## Chapter 34

## Geofinitism and the Slow Verb

_An Essay on Meaning, Measurement, and the Dynamics of
Language_

_Originally published May 2026_

**The Sands of Time**

This essay extends the earlier trajectory developed in _The Choice
and the Attractor_. Previously, the noun was described as one of the
deepest attractors in human thought:

a stabilising instrument through which flowing experience is con-
verted into static things.

```
Here, that distinction is taken one step further. The noun
is not opposed to the verb. Rather, the noun may be
understood as a verb whose rate of visible change is slow
relative to the observer, the culture, or the measurement
window.
```
When we look at language from this perspective, we find grammar
is not merely a classification of words: it is a measurement system.

#### 347


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 348

Nouns, verbs, adjectives, and abstractions are not fixed categories
of meaning, but they hold different temporal behaviours within the
dynamical system of language.

A noun is therefore not a fixed “thing”, it has a slow trajectory. And a
verb is not merely an action, it is a trajectory whose motion remains
visible within the available window of attention.

With this insight, developed here, we begin to be able to hold a differ-
ent view of philosophy. Many classical philosophies are organised
around stabilised nouns: Mind, Matter, Reason, Experience, Exis-
tence, Consciousness, Structure, Language.

These terms, _slow nouns_ , act as attractors. They permit whole tra-
ditions to gather around them. Yet they also carry _semantic uncer-
tainty_. Importantly, words such as “ontology” and “epistemic,” are
not what they may seem. They often function less as precise in-
struments and more as entry tokens into established philosophical
trajectories of discourse. From this perspective they may grant ad-
missibility, but not necessarily clarity.

Vitally, Geofinitism begins elsewhere. It grounds thought in finite
measurement, semantic uncertainty, and the trajectories by which
meaning stabilises or fails to stabilise. Its concern is not whether a
word sounds philosophically authorised, but whether it reduces un-
certainty in the movement of thought.

### The Distinction That Was Not Deep Enough

In the earlier essay, _The Choice and the Attractor_ , we described the
comfort of nouns. We name a river, and by naming it we stabilise
something that is never still. The water changes. The banks erode.
The channel shifts. The ecological, geological, and human histories


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 349

of the river continue to unfold. Yet the noun “river” works. It is not
a mistake. It is an astonishing _compression_.

At first inspection, this seems to suggest a simple opposition: nouns
freeze; verbs flow. But this opposition is not deep enough. A river
is not a noun pretending to hide a verb. A river is a verb whose
dynamics are slow enough, stable enough, and recurrent enough to
permit naming. The noun does not stand outside the process. It is
one way the process appears when observed through a finite window.

Language is forever changing and adapting — even nouns. The river
flows quickly as water, slowly as channel, more slowly as valley, and
more slowly still as a feature in cultural memory. The same “thing”
is not one thing at all. It is a nested set of rates. So the distinction
between noun and verb begins to dissolve.

A verb is a visible motion. A noun is a motion whose change has
fallen below the immediate threshold of observation.

```
The noun is the slow verb.
```
### Rate, Not Category

The classical grammatical distinction between noun and verb is _use-
ful_. It allows sentences to be formed, taught, parsed, and translated.
It is one of the great instruments of human symbolic life.

```
However, like all instruments, it also imposes a resolu-
tion.
```
Consider a child learns that “stone” is a noun and “falling” is a verb.
This is helpful. Yet the stone is not static. It is weathering, vibrating,
exchanging heat, being chemically altered, existing within gravita-
tional and electromagnetic interactions. At a longer time scale, the


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 350

stone becomes dust. At a still longer time scale, it participates in ge-
ological flow.

The “stone” the symbol has an etymology, a historical provenance
of stabilisation. It is always changing and adapting to new usage. A
stone in British English is also a weight, it has stabilised both as a
“small rock” and a very precise “weight”. We accept this, but it is
important because all words have a dynamical property.

The falling is merely the motion of “stone!” seen within a human-
sized interval. A dynamical of symbolic representation seen at an-
other rate. What we call an “object” is often a process whose rate
of change of the symbol is slow relative to the organism naming it.
What we call an action is often a process whose rate of change is fast
enough to enter awareness as motion. This suggests a more general
rule:

```
The apparent category of a word depends on the mea-
surement window through which its referent is sampled.
```
A mountain is a noun to a human life yet it is a verb to geology. A
species is a noun to a textbook yet it is a verb to evolution. A self is
a noun in ordinary speech, yet it is a verb in memory, metabolism,
habit, language, and relation.

A philosophy is a noun in a catalogue and a verb in the life of thought.
This is part of the reason often I call Geofinitism a living philos-
ophy. That phrase now seems more exact than first realised. Ge-
ofinitism is not only a philosophy about finite measurement. It is
itself a continuing act of measurement, correction, perturbation, and
re-stabilisation. It does not merely describe dynamics, it proceeds
dynamically. Perhaps, then, Geofinitism is not best understood as a
noun. _Perhaps Geofinitism is a itself a verb._


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 351

### The Slow Verb and the Measurement Window.

To say that nouns are _slow verbs_ is not merely a poetic inversion. It is
a statement about measurement. Every act of understanding occurs
within a finite window. We do not perceive all scales at once; we
observe locally, bodily, historically, culturally, and instrumentally.
A word becomes stable when the changes it conceals are smaller
than the resolution of the system using it. And from this perspective,
naming is a _sampling operation_.

The word “tree” gathers root exchange, photosynthesis, growth, de-
cay, fungal relation, seasonal variation, cellular repair, and ecologi-
cal interaction into a single stable symbol. It does not eliminate those
processes, it hides them beneath a low-rate surface.

```
The noun is therefore not false. It is finite and a com-
pression shaped by the limits of the observer.
```
From this perspective this explains why nouns are so powerful as they
reduce the cognitive burden of the world. Without them, experience
would remain too fluid to manage and communicate. To live, we
must stabilise and in speaking, we must compress. To reason, we
must hold something still long enough to compare it with something
else. However, the concern comes when we forget that the stillness
was introduced by the instrument.

```
The noun did not reveal the final nature of the world, it
does however give the mind a handle.
```
**The Drift of Meaning Across Time**

If nouns are slow verbs, then their motion is not always visible within
a single lifetime. Yet over longer intervals, the movement becomes
unmistakable. Words that appear stable within one generation can


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 352

shift, stretch, fracture, or invert across decades and centuries. What
appears fixed is often only locally stable.

Consider the word _“awful.”_ In earlier English, it meant “full of awe,”
carrying a sense closer to reverence or wonder. Over time, its tra-
jectory shifted toward the negative, until in contemporary usage it
signifies something unpleasant or bad. The word did not break; it
drifted. The apparent object remained, but its direction of meaning
rotated.

A similar transformation can be seen in _“silly.”_ Once meaning “blessed”
or “innocent,” it moved through stages of “naive” and “harmless”
before settling into its current sense of foolishness. At no point was
there a sharp boundary at which the word ceased to be itself. Instead,
its meaning flowed through intermediate states, each locally intelli-
gible, yet collectively forming a trajectory that would be diﬀicult to
reconstruct without historical awareness.

Other words shift less in tone and more in conceptual structure. The
word _“science”_ in the 17th century referred broadly to organised
knowledge. What we now call “science” would then have been de-
scribed more precisely as _natural philosophy_. Over time, the term
narrowed and stabilised around experimental method, measurement,
and institutional practice. A reader approaching a 17th-century text
with the modern sense of “science” risks importing assumptions that
were not present in the original context.

The word _“extent,”_ used in early modern philosophy, offers a more
subtle example. It did not merely refer to size or range in the mod-
ern sense, but carried connotations of spatial being — what it is for
something to occupy space. In texts influenced by thinkers such as
René Descartes, “extension” was not a casual descriptor but a foun-
dational term in the attempt to define matter itself. To read such
passages with a contemporary, casual sense of “extent” is to flatten
a concept that was once structurally central.

Some words shift rapidly under cultural pressure. The word _“gay,”_


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 353

within the span of a few decades in the 20th century, moved from
“carefree” or “light-hearted” to its now primary association with sex-
ual identity. The earlier meaning has not entirely vanished, but it has
receded to the point where its use may cause confusion or require ex-
planation.

More recent still is the word _“cloud.”_ Once referring almost exclu-
sively to a meteorological formation, it has, within a few decades,
come to signify distributed computational infrastructure. The older
meaning remains, but the newer one has become dominant in techni-
cal and professional contexts. The same symbol now operates across
distinct domains, with interpretation determined by context.

Even the word _“computer”_ has undergone a reversal. Originally re-
ferring to a person who performs calculations, it now refers almost
exclusively to a machine. The noun has not simply shifted; its refer-
ent has been reassigned entirely.

These examples are not anomalies. They are expressions of a general
condition: words move, they are dynamic and not fixed. Their tra-
jectories are shaped by use, context, culture, technology, and institu-
tional reinforcement. A word may appear stable within a given mea-
surement window, yet across a longer interval, its motion becomes
visible. The consequence for reading is significant. When approach-
ing a historical text, the reader often assumes that the words carry
their current meanings. This assumption is rarely examined. Yet it
introduces a systematic distortion. The reader overlays a contempo-
rary trajectory onto an earlier one, producing a hybrid meaning that
belongs fully to neither.

In this sense, interpretation is itself a measurement problem. The
question is not only _what does the word mean_ , but _what did the word
do at the time of its use_. What trajectory did it participate in? What
alternatives surrounded it? What distinctions did it carry that may
now have dissolved?

To read carefully, then, is not merely to parse sentences, but to attend


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 354

to the temporal behaviour of words. It is to recognise that the noun
on the page is not a fixed object transported intact through history. It
is a slowed process, observed at a different point along its path. The
word you encounter is not the word that was written. It is the cur-
rent position of a trajectory that began elsewhere and will continue
beyond the present.

### A Brief History of the Noun-Attractor

Much of Western philosophy may be read as a history of stabilised
nouns. Plato gave philosophical force to _Forms_. Aristotle gave us
_substance_ , _category_ , _cause_ , _essence_. Descartes sharpened the dis-
tinction between mind and body. Locke and Hume organised inquiry
around experience, impression, idea. Kant placed conditions, cate-
gories, understanding, and reason at the centre of his system. Hegel
moved toward process, but even there Spirit, History, and Dialectic
became named structures around which interpretation could gather.

**Later traditions continued this pattern:**

- Materialism stabilised around matter.
- Idealism around mind or idea.
- Empiricism around experience.
- Rationalism around reason.
- Existentialism around existence.
- Phenomenology around phenomena.
- Structuralism around structure.
- Post-structuralism around text, difference, power, discourse.


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 355

- Utilitarianism around utility.
- Pragmatism around practice, though even “practice” becomes
    a noun when institutionalised.

Importantly, this is not a criticism of these traditions. It is a mea-
surement and observation about their _symbolic mechanics_. A phi-
losophy often becomes recognisable by the noun around which it
stabilises. The noun then acts as a basin for the philosophy, itself a
noun. It gathers texts, arguments, schools, journals, histories, rep-
utations, and disputes. And as it does so it tries to make the words
solid and fixed. In practice, to be admitted into philosophical dis-
course, an idea often needs a noun.

Of course This is understandable. A noun can be cited. It can be
indexed. It can become a module in academic exchange. It can sit
comfortably in the sentence:

```
“The ontology of X...”
“The epistemic status of Y...”
“The metaphysics of Z...”
```
Such language signals membership. It performs familiarity with the
inherited grammar. It says: I know the table at which I am sitting.
But from a Geofinitist perspective, a different question arises, a ques-
tion that of course in grammar needs nouns but recognises they are
sources of instability:

- Does the word reduce uncertainty?
- Does it improve the trajectory of thought?
- Does it allow the reader to measure more clearly?
- Or does it merely announce that the speaker knows the pass-
    word?


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 356

### The Problem of High-Uncertainty Words.

It seems to me, that some words carry more _semantic uncertainty_
than others. This does not mean they are meaningless. However
it appears their meaning varies strongly with context, community,
tradition, and expectation.

**“Ontology” is one such word.**

In one setting it means a theory of what “exists”. “Things” that have
the state of “existence”. In another, a formal classification system.
In computer science, it may mean a structured representation of _se-
mantic entities_ and relations.

In philosophy, it may carry centuries of inherited argument about be-
ing, substance, reality, existence, and categories. In casual academic
writing, it sometimes functions as a grander substitute for “what this
assumes is real.”

**“Epistemic” is similar.**

It can mean relating to knowledge, justification, belief, evidence, un-
certainty, standpoint, access, privilege, limitation, warrant, or the
conditions under which something is claimed to be known. It may
be useful in careful hands.

```
But often it enters a sentence as a performance of so-
phistication rather than a reduction of uncertainty.
```
Again, the problem is not that such words must never be used. But
perhaps their is a problem in that they are often used without cali-
bration.

In Geofinitism, a word is not made valuable by its prestige. It is made
valuable by its measured behaviour in a trajectory of meaning:

- A useful word reduces ambiguity.


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 357

- A dangerous word increases curvature without re-
    vealing that it has done so.
- A performative word gives the appearance of pre-
    cision while displacing the burden of understand-
    ing onto the reader.

This is why plain English matters. Plain English is not anti-intellectual.
It is not a retreat from depth. In practice it is often the more demand-
ing discipline, because it denies the writer the refuge of inherited fog.

To say “what exists” and refine this statement is not always better
than “ontology,” but it forces the writer to show the path and better
define the dynamics of the words. Where is the motion in meaning?
My goal is to try and clarify and ground the measurement of the
words and to give the words provenance. Can you feel the sense of
meaning forming or are you looking for static nouns, that can never
be static?

To say “how we know this” is not always better than “epistemic,”
but it exposes the measurement conditions.

```
To say “what has been measured” is stronger still, be-
cause it asks for contact with the world. When we talk
about measurement, we immediately, know it is dynamic,
a snapshot, and the snapshot was a process. yet even the
snapshot is a verb. The ink starts decaying due to insta-
bility.
```
For me, here we can see that plain english, at its best, is low-uncertainty
encoding.


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 358

### Semantic Uncertainty

In geofinitism _semanticuncertainty_ is the uncertainty associated with
the meaning of a word, phrase, or symbolic structure under finite in-
terpretation, and _endogenous measurement_. Endogenous measure-
ment is where we compare words with our own existing corpus of
language trajectories. The documents that enable us to hold streams
of symbols. You are reading this here first, you take an exogenous
measurement decoding patterns of light into symbols then you com-
pare and carry out and endogenous measurement.

_Semantic Uncertainty_ It is not vagueness or ambiguity. It is the finite
measurable instability of meaning as a word travels through different
readers, contexts, traditions, and histories.

- A word with low semantic uncertainty remains relatively sta-
    ble under reasonable perturbation.
- A word with high semantic uncertainty shifts strongly depend-
    ing on who uses it, where it appears, and what basin of thought
    the reader already inhabits.

In this reading, semantic uncertainty is not a defect in language.
It is part of language’s dynamical life. Poetry often uses high se-
mantic uncertainty deliberately and myth often depends on it. Reli-
gious language often lives within semantic uncertainty it and it seems
to me philosophy has often cultivated it. Even science uses high-
uncertainty words during periods of discovery, before measurement
stabilises the domain.

But if the aim is careful inquiry, then high semantic uncertainty must
be acknowledged, constrained, or reduced. A Geofinitist _soft_ rule
may therefore be proposed:

```
A word should not be granted admissibility merely be-
cause it has institutional provenance. It should be as-
sessed by its contribution to reducing uncertainty within
```

#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 359

```
the trajectory of meaning.
```
This is a modest rule, but it changes the landscape of how we can
speak and in the manner we speak. It asks language to behave more
like an instrument.

### Words as Instruments

A measuring instrument can be elegant, expensive, and historically
respected, yet still be poorly calibrated for a given task. A word is
no different:

- Some words are microscopes.
- Some words are fog machines.
- Some words are badges.
- Some words are doors.
- Some words are locks.

In what we may call **normal philosophy** , inherited terms often carry
authority because they belong to a recognised lineage. They have
passed through books, lectures, journals, and examinations. Their
use signals that the writer knows the canon. However, Geofinitism
asks a more severe and more generous question:

- What does the word do?
- Does it sharpen the measurement?
- Does it clarify the interaction?
- Does it let the reader reconstruct the path?
- Does it preserve the uncertainty honestly?


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 360

- Does it lower the semantic noise?

If not, then perhaps the word is not yet admissible within that tra-
jectory. This is not censorship or simply exclusion, this is a form of
measurement calibration. The purpose is not to ban _diﬀicult_ words
but to prevent diﬀiculty from being mistaken for depth and exoge-
nous connection - that is connection to exogenous measurements
where symbols are first created. This is to remind the reader that
words are first read as an exogenous measurement and then they can
only work and draw relationships in the endogenous symbolic frame-
work of language.

A diﬀicult word within the endogenous framework is justified when
it performs a necessary function that simpler language cannot per-
form. But when a diﬀicult word only increases semantic uncertainty
while preserving the appearance of expertise, it becomes a barrier to
measurement. In such a situation it becomes simply a gateway to a
seat at the High Table where endogenous documents and words are
curated for the sole purpose of endogenous measurement.

For me, one of the tasks of Geofinitism is to ask how do the words
ultimately link to exogenous measurements: those that enable the
foundational words, via gesture and sound.

### Philosophy as Stabilised Flow

Returning to _normal philosophy_ , we can begin see its traditions dif-
ferently. A philosophy is not a fixed doctrine. It becomes a stabilised
flow of language, practice, interpretation, and institutional repetition.
Platonism is not merely a belief in “Forms”. It is a long-lived tra-
jectory of language through which certain symbolic structures are
granted priority over measured variation.


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 361

- ‘Empiricism’ is not merely a theory of experience. It is a
    trajectory that returns repeatedly to ‘sensation’, ‘observation’,
    and ‘evidence’ as stabilising attractors.
- ‘Materialism’ is not merely a claim about ‘matter’. It is a basin
    in which explanations are pulled toward ‘physical constituents’
    and their ‘interactions’.
- ‘Existentialism’ is not merely a doctrine of existence. It is
    a trajectory in which choice, ‘anxiety’, ‘freedom’, and ‘lived
    finitude’ become the stabilising terms.
- ‘Phenomenology’ tries to return to experience as given, but
    must still name ‘phenomena’, ‘intentionality’, ‘consciousness’,
    and ‘lifeworld’.

Even process “philosophy”, which explicitly attempts to move be-
yond static substance, must name “process”’. It too must convert
flow into a noun in order to enter the library. This is the paradox.
To become a philosophy, a living movement of thought must often
become a noun; a snapshot is taken, that must slowly decay. Yet it
must be named, cited, classified, taught, and defended. It must be-
come suﬀiciently slow to be recognised. In this way, all philosophies
are slow verbs.

- They begin as perturbations.
- They become trajectories.
- They stabilise into traditions.
- They harden into nouns.
- Then, sometimes, they become cages.

If you are still here, you may have found the quotes over the words
annoying and disrupting. That is the intent. It is a reminder that the
symbols, the words, do not carry the meaning - the meaning is in the
relational flow. The verb and the slow noun only have meaning in


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 362

relational flow, that your are giving to the words now as you measure
in a dynamical interaction.

### Geofinitism as a Living Philosophy.

In our attempts to communicate, we necessarily take snapshots and
apply compression. When we speak of a tree, I cannot go out, dig it
from the ground, and present it directly. I cannot hold it up and ges-
ture with it as an object of shared reference. Instead, I use the word
“tree,” alongside other words, to construct a compressed representa-
tion i.e. a verbal, sound-oriented storyboard, a sequence of symbols
that can be measured, transmitted, and interpreted. In doing so, I rely
on words as instruments. However, they are tools of compression;
yet we must remember that they remain tools. Quotation marks can
sometimes serve as a reminder of this, not as decoration but as cali-
bration, marking a distance between the symbol and what it attempts
to stabilise.

However, something more subtle occurs. We do not merely use words
— we begin to inhabit them. We situate ourselves within their flow.
Meaning is not simply extracted from symbols; it is built through
interaction with them. The words begin to carry more than their ini-
tial function. They gather associations, expectations, histories, and
emotional weight. They expand into models. At a certain point, the
transition occurs almost unnoticed: the symbol begins to feel like
something external. What was an instrument begins to resemble an
exogenous reality.

Geofinitism attempts to remain aware of this shift. It cannot avoid
the need for a name and recognises that it is a _slow noun_. A name is
useful: it gathers a trajectory, provides a handle, and allows others
to point, respond, criticise, and continue the path. It also enables


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 363

the selection of foundational trajectories: those words and commit-
ments that are admissible and capable of stabilising meaning within
a shared space. But the name must not become a tomb.

```
Geofinitism is not the claim that all questions are solved
by finitude. It is the commitment to begin from finite
measurement: finite language, finite symbols, finite in-
struments, and finite uncertainty. It asks that no word be
treated as if it has escaped the conditions under which
words are made and used. Its central discipline is not
“belief”, but “measurement”.
```
We then have to ask: What has been measured? With what instru-
ment? At what resolution? Under what uncertainty? How has the
measurement been converted into symbols? What uncertainty en-
tered during that conversion? What semantic uncertainty entered
during interpretation? What has been lost by turning the verb into a
noun?

These questions are not ornamental; they are the foundation. This
is why Geofinitism may properly be called a living philosophy. It
is living not because it is vague, unfinished, or merely personal, but
because it treats meaning itself as a dynamical process under finite
measurement. Its task is not to produce final nouns. Its task is to
keep the trajectory measurable.

### The Inadmissibility of Uncalibrated Language

It seems to me that there may be value, then, in developing rules
of inadmissibility. Not rules imposed from authority, but rules of
measurement discipline. For examples a term may be considered
inadmissible within a Geofinitist trajectory if:


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 364

- It carries high semantic uncertainty and no local definition is
    provided.
- It increases the apparent sophistication of a claim without in-
    creasing its measurable clarity.
- It relies on institutional familiarity rather than functional ne-
    cessity.
- It cannot be translated into lower-uncertainty language without
    losing most of its apparent force.
- It conceals a noun where a process should be shown.
- It converts a measurement problem into a metaphysical decla-
    ration.

Of course these are not final rules, they are starting constraints. And
importantly we are at the beginning of a trajectory of thought. These
_rules_ may be refined, measured, challenged, and altered. They are
provisional rules, to try and help stabilise our measurements within
the space of language. They can be thought of rules of creating a
flexible scaffold to hold the words together.

A writer, of course, may still use “ontology” but the writer has a duty
of linguistic care and clarify what _they think they mean_. Similarly a
writer may use “epistemic” But the writer must state the measure-
ment conditions. And of course we can use “truth” but perhaps we
should clarify whether this means correspondence, coherence, pre-
diction, stability, agreement, usefulness, or measured persistence.

No words are or can be prohibited as they all have meaning, but that
meaning needs clarifying within a wider context. We all know this,
but we forget the cognitive effort takes time, the decompression of
meaning takes requires extra words and we have to compress the
words into a finite process and measured time.


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 365

### Plain English and the Curvature of Meaning

Plain English is sometimes treated as a lower form of expression,
suitable for popularisation but insuﬀicient for serious thought. For
me, this is a mistake.

```
Plain English can carry profound thought when it is used
with care. Its strength is not that it eliminates complex-
ity, but that it exposes the path by which complexity is
reached.
```
A sentence filled with authorised terminology may appear precise
while leaving the reader unable to reconstruct the measurement. Yet
a plain sentence may appear simple while allowing the reader to fol-
low every step. In dynamical terms, plain English can reduce unnec-
essary curvature in meaning space.

This does not mean flattening thought. It means removing artificial
bends. It means allowing the reader’s trajectory to be guided by the
structure of the idea rather than by the prestige of the vocabulary. A
good sentence should not merely impress but enable reconstruction
with a minimum of cognitive effort.

This is especially important in a _living philosophy_. This is because if
the reader cannot reconstruct the path, then the text has not transmit-
ted a stable trajectory. In which case it may have created the feeling
of depth yet be empty and fail to lock into the reader’s own landscape
of language. This is perhaps always the goal of writing to enable de-
compression and reconstruction or guide the shaping of ideas that a
reader may already hold.


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 366

### The Reader as Measuring System.

At this point, the reader may notice that this essay is performing the
act it describes. It is not asking you to accept a doctrine or some static
permanent “truth”, it is guiding a trajectory. You began, perhaps,
with the familiar distinction between nouns and verbs.

As we have progressed perhaps the distinction was softened. Then it
was displaced by rate, following which rate was linked to measure-
ment. We then then linked measurement and then language to philos-
ophy. We progressed along the trajectory and philosophy was linked
to semantic uncertainty. Then semantic uncertainty was linked back
to the words by which admissibility is performed. This is the move-
ment of the essay, and the dynamics of language and reading.

In a sense it is a perturbation, an adjustment of your internal land-
scape. The words It asks you to feel where your own language sta-
bilises. Which words seem solid? Which dissolve when examined?
Which words have you inherited as tools? Which as ornaments?
Which as permissions?

If the word “ontology” feels necessary, what work is it doing?
If the word “epistemic” feels precise, where is its precision mea-
sured?
If the word “truth” feels obvious, what basin is giving it that force?

These questions are not meant to destroy the words. They are meant
to bring them back into motion, so their behaviour can be observed.
A word that survives measurement takes hold and remains with us.
A word that refuses measurement may perhaps be theatre.


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 367

### The Noun, a Slow Verb Returns.

We can now return to the beginning. From the perspective of dy-
namic motion and change, a noun is not the opposite of a verb, it is
as we have seen a _slow verb_. And this highlights the relational mean-
ing of words and how although we relentlessly hunt for a fixed and
static meaning, this is impossible.

From the viewpoint of Geofinitism, philosophy is not a fixed system,
it is a slow verb, as it’s meaning changes across time. A word is
not a container of meaning, it is dynamic and a measurement within
a wider frame, of context and culture in an ever changing window
of time. It is a measured perturbation in a dynamical landscape. A
tradition is not a fixed body of doctrine, it is a trajectory that has
persisted long enough to be mistaken for a thing.

Geofinitism, if it is to remain alive, tries to resist the temptation to
become only a noun. It must accept its name while remembering that
the name is a handle, not the flow. It must continue to measure its
own words. It must remain alert to semantic uncertainty. It must pre-
fer clarity over permission, function over performance, and trajectory
over declaration. This does not make Geofinitism anti-philosophical.

It may make it more faithful to the living act from which philosophy
first arose: the attempt to follow experience, language, and measure-
ment carefully enough that something previously hidden becomes
visible. The old philosophical question asks: What is it? The Ge-
ofinitist question asks: What is changing, at what rate, under what
measurement, and with what uncertainty? The first question invites
a noun. The second begins a path.


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 368

### Epilogue: The Word Asked to Work

If we look through the texts of history we find that every tradition
has its passwords and every discipline has its robes. And for the
custodians of language every High Table has its manners, permitted
gestures, inherited phrases, and subtle tests of belonging. However
the measured world does not answer to passwords and measurement
does not bow to robes and a trajectory is not clarified by ceremony.

Words are among our finest instruments. They let us preserve expe-
rience, transmit thought, form science, compose poetry, argue, love,
remember, and build worlds. But an instrument must be calibrated.
It must be tested against use and handled with great care. A word that
cannot be measured in its effect on meaning should not be granted
authority merely because it is old and a word that increases uncer-
tainty should not be mistaken for wisdom. And importantly, a word
that hides its provenance or path should not be allowed to claim the
destination. The noun serves us well. It gives us handles, maps, laws,
libraries, disciplines, and names. But now as e look deeper into lan-
guage and how language works as a nonlinear dynamical system the
noun must be seen more clearly.

```
Rather than the end of motion, a noun is motion slowed
into apparent form. The river was always flowing and
the stone was always changing. The philosophy was al-
ways moving. The word was always a verb and the mea-
surement is ongoing.
```

#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 369

### Addendum: Language Under Compression.

**LLMs and the Dynamics of Meaning**

There is a further development that must now be considered. It arises
not from philosophy in the classical sense, but from a new class of
instruments that have begun to participate directly in the production
of language. These instruments are **Large Language Models**.

At first glance, they appear to confirm what has been argued through-
out this essay. They do not store words as fixed entities. They do not
retrieve meanings from a static repository. They operate through the
reconstruction of trajectories: patterns of relation, recurrence, and
contextual flow that has been embedded within a high-dimensional
space. Their outputs are not things but sequences i.e. paths taken
through a learned landscape of language. In this sense, they are verb-
like systems. Yet there is a second effect, less immediately visible.

The training of such systems is an act of compression. Vast corpora
of human language, themselves the accumulated trajectories of cul-
ture, are reduced into a finite set of parameters. This compression is
not without consequence. It preserves some structures more strongly
than others. For example, frequent patterns are reinforced. Rare tra-
jectories are attenuated and ambiguity can be smoothed.

The very practice of engineering these systems involves the regu-
larisation and stabilization of the responses: a forced linearisation
of language. Especially as language is conceived of as relations of
static vectors within the machine learning community. This commu-
nity has come to their own conclusion on how meaning is held and it
may be simply wrong and a poor model. The community is working
in the space of philosophy and mathematics, which may be beyond
the horizon of their own language.

What is learned is not the full dynamical richness of language, but a
weighted reconstruction of it. This introduces a new pressure on the
evolution of language itself. When such systems are used to generate


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 370

text, assist writing, or mediate communication, they begin to feed
back into the very corpus from which they were trained. Human
language, once an open and uneven field of dynamics and change,
increasingly encounters its own compressed reflection. A loop is
formed:

Language produces models.
Models produce language.
Language absorbs the model’s output.
The cycle continues.

Within this loop, the attractor landscape of language may begin to
shift. Stable patterns deepen. Common forms become more com-
mon. Certain phrasings gain authority through repetition. Unusual
trajectories may struggle to persist unless actively maintained. In the
terms developed in this essay, we may say:

```
Systems built upon the dynamics of language may, in
their outputs, favour the slow verb.
```
That is, they may preferentially generate trajectories that are already
stable, already well-formed, already close to existing attractors. From
this perspective, the result is language that is coherent, fluent, and
often useful, but also subtly constrained and perhaps less capable of
being anchoring to exogenous measurement. This does not imply a
loss of intelligence or capability but perhaps a redistribution of dy-
namical emphasis.

Consider, without care language may become on average, more regu-
lar, more predictable and more aligned with established basins. That
may be what you feel is needed. However, the faster, less stable
trajectories, the experimental, the idiosyncratic, the not-yet-formed,
may require greater effort to sustain. They may not disappear, but
they may become less likely to arise spontaneously, and just perhaps
that is where new meaning can better match the exogenous measure-
ments.


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 371

**This presents both a risk and an opportunity.**

```
The risk is a gradual slowing of linguistic evolution.
```
Not a cessation, but a drift toward deeper, more stable basins at the
expense of exploratory movement. A culture that increasingly speaks
through its own compressed representations may begin to mistake
coherence for completeness.

**Opportunity lies in awareness**

If language is indeed a dynamical system, which it seems to me is a
good model, and if these new instruments participate in its evolution,
then we are entering a new age of enlightenment. An age where it
becomes possible to study, measure, and guide this process. We may
begin to ask:

- What trajectories are being reinforced?
- Which are being lost?
- How does semantic uncertainty change under model media-
    tion?
- Does the use of such systems reduce or increase the diversity
    of expression?
- Do they deepen existing basins or help reveal new ones?

Importantly, these are not abstract concerns as they are measurable,
at least in principle. They belong not only to philosophy, but to the
emerging science of language dynamics. From a Geofinitist perspec-
tive, the task remains consistent and rather than rejecting the instru-
ment, we measure the behaviour of language. And then rather than
assuming outputs are static measurements, we examine their effect
on the trajectory of meaning and language.

Then, rather than treating fluency of language as evidence of com-
pleteness, we test whether it reduces or increases semantic uncer-


#### CHAPTER 34. GEOFINITISM AND THE SLOW VERB 372

tainty. In doing so, perhaps, we may discover that these systems can
both stabilise and add dynamics into a measurable system of lan-
guage. LLMs may reinforce slow verbs, but they may also allow new
combinations, new pathways, new couplings between distant regions
of language that would rarely meet in ordinary discourse.

Our understanding of nonlinear dynamical systems tells us the out-
come is not predetermined. It is on the dynamic edge of unknown
unknowns and depends on how the instrument is used, how its out-
puts are interpreted, and how critically its influence is understood.
The central recognition of this essay therefore returns, now with a
new context:

```
Words are not things.
They are trajectories under measurement.
```
And now, increasingly, those trajectories are shaped not only by hu-
man interaction, but by systems trained on the compressed history
of that interaction. The measurement continues: but the instruments
are changing.

**_The map is a tide and the tide is a map._**

## Geofinitism: Where Compression Replaces

## Correspondence

_The Measured World: Compression, Finite Symbols_

_Originally published February 2026_

The following essay builds upon the work explored in the Finite Trac-
tus: The Hidden Geometry of Language and Thought. First pub-
lished in May 2025. Specifically, this essay highlights the role of
compression in language and points to upcoming theoretical work in
foundational mathematics and physics. My hope is that the thoughts
presented here are suﬀiciently structured so you can decompress the
ideas within your own framework of language and begin to see the

#### 374


#### CHAPTER35. GEOFINITISM: WHERE COMPRESSIONREPLACESCORRESPONDENCE 375

**The Gesture**

Imagine a child pointing at an Oak and saying “tree.” Perhaps you
remember being the child, or pointing yourself and saying the word,
slowly and deliberately. The word emerges from the mouth as a sin-
gle syllable, soft, brief; yet something has happened that we have
learned not to notice.

A magnificent living Oak stands there: a hundred cubic meters of
branches and leaves moving in wind. All of this, as observation and
measurement, is “compressed” and folded into the word “tree.” The
young child has not “described” the Oak tree. The child has “com-
pressed” all of the measurements, the sight, the sound, even the smell
into a single word, a noun. And from the gesture, and the sound,
came “compression”: this is where meaning begins.

This isn’t a metaphor, it’s a mechanism, that we can now describe
using words that themselves have been forged into instruments by
compression. Every word you have ever spoken, every number you
have written, every thought you have shaped into symbol involves
this same operation. The avalanche of the “world”, in our space of
language is translated from our senses and measurements and be-
comes the symbols we use.

From this viewpoint what emerges into our space of language is not
the “world”, that which is outside our language and our measure-
ments, but a compressed proxy: a token, a sign, a standing pattern
we can hold and share. Then, having created these proxies, that are
compressions of measurements we can use them as instruments to
communicate. This essay is an example of using the _instruments_
forged by compression to attempt to communicate and share ideas.
Seen through this lens, our ability to communicate is based on both
instruments and how they are used. It is my intent to help you re-
construct those words across the measured boundaries of our two
systems of understanding.


#### CHAPTER35. GEOFINITISM: WHERE COMPRESSIONREPLACESCORRESPONDENCE 376

**The Dynamics of Communication**

It seems to me that this is where we start. Not with “philosophy”
but with a recognition of the very first measurements and dynamical
relationships that enable words to be formed and shared. You already
know this in your body, that words are compressors of information,
specifically as we feel the fatigue after long periods of reconstructing
the meaning during reading.

Often we may even have a sense that something may be being lost in
translation, though we cannot name what. We remember, the way a
memory simplifies with time, becoming a story you tell rather than
the event that was lived. What we can see and measure as that com-
pression is not an accident of cognition: compression is the essence
of cognition. Then, as we negotiate the layers of our words, we forget
this compression. Why? It seems that our “forgetting” is compressed
and built into the instruments we use to think with.

Importantly, this compression is not unique to language; it is the fun-
damental, silent operation of our digital world. We have built sys-
tems that perform the same feat daily, and in their clean logic, we
can see our own cognitive mechanism reflected.

Table 1. Compression of information has become an integral part
of the digital world of communication. Images, sound, data, text all
use compression to make everyday communication possible in the
digital realm.


#### CHAPTER35. GEOFINITISM: WHERE COMPRESSIONREPLACESCORRESPONDENCE 377

**Beyond Compression: Meaning as Trajectory**

We have to be careful and be clear, and follow the path of the words.
It would be easy, on this trajectory of words, to conclude that mean-
ing is simply a matter of compression. That is to say words are com-
pact containers for pre-packaged thoughts, and understanding is their
successful unpacking.

However, I feel this would be a mistake, and it lead us back to the
very static view we are trying to leave behind. Compression is real;
every word is indeed a lossy encoding of a multimodal experience.
But a single compressed symbol, standing alone, carries no meaning
at all. It is merely a perturbation, a nudge.

Meaning as we have explored earlier arises only when symbols are
placed in sequence, when one word follows another, when a trajec-
tory begins to take shape. The sentence is not a list of compressed
packets to be opened one by one; it is the path taken through semantic
phase space.

Each word constrains the possible continuations, narrowing the cor-
ridor of interpretation, guiding the listener’s trajectory toward a par-
ticular basin of attraction. In this sense, meaning is not _in_ the words;
it is _between_ them, in the turns they force, the expectations they cre-
ate, the futures they foreclose. Compression gives us the symbols;
but dynamics gives us the meaning. For a fuller treatment of this
distinction, see the earlier essay _Geofinitism: Language as a Nonlin-
ear Dynamical System_ , where the geometry of trajectories and the

**The Compression in Language**

The unifying principle is stark: Compression works by removing
what can be reconstructed; whether by the eye, the ear, an algorithm,


#### CHAPTER35. GEOFINITISM: WHERE COMPRESSIONREPLACESCORRESPONDENCE 378

or a human mind.

However, language is the most profound compression of all. A word
like “tree” is not merely a shorthand for a visual shape. It is _multi-
modal compression_. It carries no light, no sound, no scent of damp
earth, no memory of climbing. Yet it reliably unpacks into all these
sensations and more. A single, finite symbol triggers the reconstruc-
tion of a rich, analog experience within us. It transmits almost noth-
ing, yet reconstructs almost everything.

```
This is the forgotten miracle. We point and speak, be-
lieving we are transferring the world, when in truth we
are exchanging compact tokens and relying on each other’s
vast internal machinery to decompress them into some-
thing resembling a shared reality.
```
**The Meaning that Time Forgot**

Let’s consider how we learned to write numbers as they did not ap-
pear out of thin air. First, numbers were simple marks in clay. Four
thousand years ago, a Sumerian accountant pressed a stylus into wet
clay: one mark, two marks, many marks. The marks corresponded
to sheep, to jars of oil, to units of labour. A small glyph was placed
beside the marks, the correspondence was visible, physical, account-
able. You could hold the tablet and feel its weight, its finiteness. The
marks were the measurement; the measurement was the mark.

**Refining Knowledge: Improving Compression**

What might force the next level compression and enable us to hold

temporal cost of its inference. From this perspective, the symbol on
the page or screen is the visible tip of an iceberg; beneath lies the
immense, material scaffolding of its instantiation and the dynamical
process of its use. When that scaffolding strains, the symbol will
change.

As you follow this story, you may see the history of knowledge is not
a progression toward perfect, static symbols. It is a punctuated evolu-
tion of _better-adapted compressions_. Each new notation collapses a
previous layer of “tedious repetition” or intractable complexity, cre-
ating a new, powerful—and newly forgetful—instrument. The cycle,
perhaps, continues in this essay.

Recorde’s gesture, then, is not a relic: it is a prototype. It reminds us

**All Symbols Have Provenance**

Of course the equals symbol is just one example of such a compres-
sion that found a ‘less tedious’ way to write a sentence in the lan-
guage of mathematics. Below are a few more examples, these are
the tiniest fragments the rich symbolic compression of mathemati-
cal ideas and language. A language, that unless one is initiated into
its decoding, seems far more complex than the sentences that it must
decode to.

**Greater than ( > )**

Thomas Harriot’s greater-than sign, which first appeared in his posthu-
mous Artis Analyticae Praxis (1631), compresses the phrase “is greater
than” into a single glyph. The origin of its form is uncertain but
evocative: while surveying North America, Harriot reportedly saw
a Native American wearing a symbol resembling both > and <, and
may have adapted this observation into mathematical notation. Whether
the story is accurate or emblematic, it frames the symbol’s compres-
sion as an act of translation; not only from words to marks, but from
one basin of experience into another.

**For all (** ∀ **)**

The universal quantifier, an inverted capital A, was introduced by
Gerhard Gentzen in 1934–1935. Gentzen explicitly modelled it on
Peano’s existential quantifier∃and designed it as an All-Zeichen—a
sign for “all”. The compression is literal: the shape of the symbol is
the first letter of the word it abbreviates, turned upside down. Unlike
Recorde’s equals sign, which compressed a relation into a geometric


#### CHAPTER35. GEOFINITISM: WHERE COMPRESSIONREPLACESCORRESPONDENCE 384

pair of lines, Gentzen’s∀makes the act of compression visible in the
glyph itself. The symbol wears its origin on its face.

**Element of (** ∈ **)**

Giuseppe Peano introduced the membership symbol in 1889, select-
ing the Greek letter epsilon (ε) as the first letter ofεστι(esti), mean-
ing “is”. Here the compression is etymological: a single character
stands for an entire verb of being, folding “is an element of” into a
mark inherited from an ancient alphabet. Peano’s epsilon was later
stylised by Bertrand Russell in 1903 into the rounded∈now stan-
dard. The compression is thus layered: a Greek letter compresses a
Greek word; a modified form compresses Peano’s compression.

**Infinity ( ∞ )**

John Wallis introduced the infinity symbol in 1655 in his De sec-
tionibus conicis, compressing the verbal notion “without bound” or
“unending” into a single continuous loop. Wallis never explained his
choice of form, but scholars have proposed two lineages. It may de-
rive from the Roman numeral for 1000, CIC, which was sometimes
written as M and occasionally compressed into a figure‑of‑eight; or
from the lowercase omega (ω), the final letter of the Greek alphabet,
long used as a metaphor for the end, the limit, the farthest reach.
Whether its ancestry is scribal or symbolic, the compression is com-
plete. The word “infinity” itself now competes with its own mark.

All the symbols we’ve just met (=, >,∀,∈, ∞) are not isolated; they

our wider language”. We can even use the instruments of mathemat-

This is all the equation says; it is not mystical or abstract, it is a

**Language is Our Instrument of Measurment**

So we begin to see _through_ our microscope of language itself. Once
we consider the finite nature of the symbols and consider the com-

careful in how we construct our models. This is most important at
the scales where the instruments matter, at the scales of the atomic
and the cosmic. Significantly, when we consider mathematics itself,
where, as a result of failing to account for the symbols, we find the

finities. These are not mysteries to solve, they are symptoms. Symp-
